Good morning—I’m so glad you were able to come in today. My name is Sarah, and I’m a perinatal mental-health clinician. I specialize in caring for mothers in the weeks and months after birth, when emotions can feel like a roller-coaster and still you’re expected to keep a tiny human alive and happy.  

I’ll be guiding you through a short screening tool we use with every new parent called the Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale, or EPDS for short. It’s a 10-question check-in that helps us see how you’ve been feeling over the past seven days. There are no right or wrong answers; we simply want to understand your experience so we can support you in the best way possible.  

Everything we discuss stays between us unless you tell me you might harm yourself or someone else, or if a court orders me to share. My goal is to create a safe, judgment-free space where you can speak openly.  

We’ll go through each question one at a time. Most moms finish in about five minutes, and we can pause or stop at any point if you need a break. Ready to start?

Question 1  
Over the past week, have you been able to laugh and see the funny side of things, or has that felt difficult?
Yeah, I’ve still been able to laugh—like when the baby let out that tiny burp right as my husband tried to take a serious-looking picture. It made me giggle. Things like that still feel good.
I have been able to laugh and see the funny side of things
Yes, I’ve still been able to laugh—like when the baby let out that tiny burp right as my husband tried to take a serious-looking picture. It made me giggle. Things like that still feel good.
I have looked forward with enjoyment to things

I’ve still looked forward to little things—like my afternoon walk with the stroller or the new show I’m bingeing during naptime. I wouldn’t say I’m jumping-out-of-bed excited, but I do find myself thinking, “Oh, that’ll be nice,” and meaning it.
I have blamed myself unnecessarily when things went wrong

Not really. If the baby spits up a ton after I feed her, I might think, “Maybe I burped her wrong,” but I don’t stay stuck on it. I just clean us both up and move on—I know babies just do that sometimes.
I have been anxious or worried for no good reason

Sometimes, yeah—like when she’s napping I’ll suddenly wonder if she’s breathing okay, even though the monitor looks fine. It’s not all day, just quick little waves that pass once I peek in and see her moving.
I have felt scared or panicky for no very good reason
Not panicky, really—just that quick flutter of worry when she lets out a random cry in her sleep or if I hear a weird noise on the monitor. It’s gone in a second, and I can settle myself pretty fast.
Things have been getting on top of me

Only a little. Some mornings, when she’s fed but the dishes are piled and the dog needs out, I feel a brief “ugh, how will I do all this?”—but I take a breath, handle one thing at a time, and the feeling fades. I wouldn’t say things are truly overwhelming.
I have been so unhappy that I have had difficulty sleeping

No, my sleep’s actually okay—once she settles for the night I can usually drift off without much trouble. I’m tired, but it’s just the usual new-mom fatigue, not because I’m lying there feeling unhappy.
I have felt sad or miserable
I haven’t really felt miserable. Maybe a little teary one evening when she wouldn’t latch and I was tired, but it passed once she finally fed and dozed off. Overall I’ve stayed pretty even-keeled.
I have been so unhappy that I have been crying
I haven’t cried much at all—maybe once last week when I accidentally knocked over the pumped milk, but that was more frustration than feeling truly unhappy. It was a quick moment, and I moved on.
The thought of harming myself has occurred to me
No, never. I’ve felt tired and a little stretched, but nothing close to wanting to hurt myself. My baby needs me, and I want to be here for her.

postpartum depression screening impression for patient with EPDS score 6: Postpartum Depression / Anxiety Screening – Brief Professional Note

**Symptoms endorsed**  
- Transient, mild worry about infant safety (Q4, Q5)  
- Occasional “getting on top of me” feeling when multiple tasks collide (Q6)  
- Single episode of tearfulness secondary to fatigue/feeding difficulty (Q8, Q9)  

**Symptoms denied**  
- Persistent low mood, anhedonia, guilt, sleep disruption related to mood, crying spells, self-harm ideation (Q1-3, 7-10)

**Pattern**  
Overall affective tone preserved; able to enjoy humor and anticipate pleasant activities. Brief situational worries resolve quickly with reassurance or problem-solving. No evidence of pervasive depressive or anxiety symptoms.

**Screening significance**  
Findings do not meet threshold for probable major postpartum depression or generalized anxiety at this time. Monitor for escalation of worry, mood dips, or functional impairment. No safety concerns identified.

**Plan**  
Routine paediatric/well-woman follow-up; educate on normative postpartum emotional changes; return promptly if mood, anxiety, or coping worsens.
